chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to me who said: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Isfahani narrated to me, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Manquri, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the battles of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), and the asker was from our lovers. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: Indeed, God the Exalted sent Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) with five swords.

Three of them are unsheathed and will not be sheathed until war lays down its burdens, and war will not lay down its burdens until the sun rises from its setting place. When the sun rises from the west, all people will be safe on that day. On that day, the faith of a soul will not benefit it if it had not believed before or earned good through its faith.
One of them is wrapped up, and one of them is sheathed; we drew it for others, but its ruling is entrusted to us.

As for the three unsheathed swords: The first sword is against the Arab polytheists. God the Blessed and Exalted said: 'So kill the polytheists wherever you find them and seize them and besiege them and lie in wait for them in every place.' If they repent and establish prayer and give zakat...

These are not accepted from them except [by] the sword or killing, or entering Islam, and they have no booty (fay'). Their children are captives, as the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) did; for he captured and pardoned, and accepted ransom.

The second sword is against the People of the Covenant (Ahl al-Dhimmah). God the Exalted said: 'Speak good to people.' This was revealed regarding the People of the Covenant, then it was abrogated by His saying: 'Fight those who do not believe in God or the Last Day, nor forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, nor follow the religion of truth, from those who were given the Scripture, until they pay the jizyah with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.'

Whoever of them is in the House of Islam is not accepted from him except the jizyah or killing. If they accept the jizyah upon themselves, it becomes forbidden for us to capture them, their wealth becomes protected, and marriage to their women becomes permissible for us. Whoever of them is in the House of War, their capture and wealth are permissible for us, but marriage to them is not permissible, and they are not accepted except by killing or entering Islam.

And a sword against the non-Arab polytheists, meaning the Turks, the Daylamites, and the Khazars. God the Exalted said in the Surah of Those Who Disbelieved: 'So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike [their] necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter among them, then bind a bond firmly. Then either [afterward a] favor or ransom.'

Meaning the exchange/ransom between them and the people of Islam. These are not accepted from them except by killing or entering Islam, and marriage to them is not permissible for us as long as they are in the House of War.

As for the wrapped sword: It is the sword against the rebels and those of interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'wil). God the Blessed and Exalted said: 'And if two parties of the believers fight, then make settlement between the two. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of God.'

When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is among you one who will fight after me regarding interpretation as I fought regarding revelation.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, who is he?' He said: 'The one who mends his shoe,' meaning the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him).

And 'Ammar ibn Yasir said: 'I fought under this banner with the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) and his household three times, and this is the fourth (time). By God, even if they drove us back as far as the date plantations of Hajar, we would know that we are upon the truth and they are upon falsehood.'

The conduct of the Commander of the Faithful towards them was as the conduct of the Messenger of God towards the people of Mecca on the day of its conquest; for he did not capture their offspring, and he said: 'Whoever closes his door and casts aside his weapon or enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe.'

And so did the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) say regarding them on the day of Basra: 'Do not capture their offspring, do not finish off the wounded, and do not pursue the fleeing. Whoever closes his door and casts aside his weapon is safe.'

As for the sheathed sword: It is the sword with which retaliation (Qisas) is established. God the Exalted said: 'Life for life.' We draw it for the heirs of the slain, and its ruling is entrusted to us.

These are the swords with which God the Exalted sent His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). Whoever denies them or denies anything [of them] or their conduct and rulings has indeed disbelieved in what God revealed to Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family).

key_terms.أَهْلُ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the Covenant (non-Muslims living under Islamic rule)
key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبَغْيِ: The rebels (those who revolt against the Imam)
key_terms.التَّأْوِيلُ: Interpretation (referring to the specific context of the rebel's claim)
key_terms.مَغْمُودٌ: Sheathed (drawn by others, ruled by Imams)

ai.seo_question: What are the five swords of authority and warfare mentioned in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal outlines the five categories of jihad, distinguishing between the perpetual 'unsheathed' swords against polytheists and the People of the Book, and the specific 'wrapped' sword of al-Bagh (rebellion) linked to Imam Ali’s campaigns. It further clarifies the 'sheathed' sword of Qisas, emphasizing the Imams' authority in its application, while noting the theological weight of denying these distinct juridical categories. The text highlights the continuity of prophetic practice in Imam Ali’s conduct during the Battle of the Camel, reinforcing the Shia view of his just governance.
